analysis.one_liner: Protects abortion access nationwide by barring state restrictions on patients and providers.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 219-210 on July 15, 2022 — every voting Democrat but one in favor, every voting Republican against — but the Senate never voted before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced three weeks after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, the bill would create a federal statutory right to abortion. States and local governments could not ban abortion before fetal viability, impose waiting periods, mandatory tests, telemedicine bans, or clinic regulations that single out abortion providers, and could not ban abortion after viability when the provider judges the pregnancy risks the patient's life or health. The Justice Department, patients, and providers could sue to enforce it, and states could not claim immunity. The House passed it on a near party-line vote; the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: People who can become pregnant — especially those with low incomes, people in states with bans or heavy restrictions, and rural residents, whom the bill's findings note sometimes travel more than 100 miles to reach a provider. The bill's findings also emphasize that restrictions fall hardest on Black, Indigenous, and other people of color, immigrants, young people, and people with disabilities. Abortion clinics and their staff gain a protected right to practice without abortion-specific regulations and a federal cause of action against state interference, with attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing abortion care and their providers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal statutory right to abortion before fetal viability, and after viability when the treating provider judges the pregnancy risks the patient's life or health — and it applies retroactively, striking down state bans already on the books.

Bars the most common state restrictions: mandatory ultrasounds and other tests not required for medically comparable procedures, medically inaccurate counseling scripts, unnecessary in-person visits before care, telemedicine bans, and limits on prescribing medication abortion based on current evidence-based regimens.

Strikes down targeted clinic regulations — building, staffing, and hospital-transfer requirements or credentialing rules — that apply only to abortion providers and not to medically comparable outpatient procedures.

Gives patients and providers standing to sue states and officials, abrogates state immunity, awards attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs, and treats anyone authorized to enforce a violating restriction — such as private citizens deputized by state law — as a government official subject to suit.

analysis.who_pays: State governments and the officials who enforce abortion restrictions lose authority over the field, face civil suits from the Justice Department and private plaintiffs, and would have to unwind restrictions enacted before the bill. Taxpayers absorb the cost of the resulting federal and state litigation. The bill explicitly leaves insurance and Medicaid coverage rules untouched, so it does not change what insurers cover.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law and applies to restrictions enacted before its passage, so it would invalidate bans and limits that state legislatures — and in some states the voters themselves — had adopted, overriding state-level democratic decisions on a divisive question.

The legal burden sits heavily on governments: a state can defend a restriction only by proving with clear and convincing evidence that it significantly advances patient safety and that no less restrictive alternative exists, and viability is defined by the treating provider's good-faith judgment — leaving states little room to regulate even later in pregnancy, which goes beyond simply restoring the pre-2022 framework.

It removes legal barriers but not financial ones: insurance and medical assistance coverage of abortion is explicitly excluded from the bill, so care becomes lawful without becoming affordable for low-income patients.

Enforcement invites recurring litigation: any adversely affected person or entity can sue states and officials, with attorney's fees paid to prevailing plaintiffs and no fee liability for non-frivolous claims, so states would face repeated courtroom challenges to their laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in the roughly half of states the bill's findings predicted would ban abortion after the Court's ruling, the bill would restore access the Court had just withdrawn, and the National Academies review cited in the bill found abortion is safe and that state-specific regulations are the biggest threat to care quality. The honest cost is to federalism: the bill reaches back to strike down restrictions those states chose, and its provider-defined viability standard and clear-and-convincing-evidence burden go further than a simple return to prior law. It also does nothing about cost or coverage, so for poor patients legality does not guarantee access. The preemption design is why every Senate Republican and at least one House Democrat opposed it, and why the bill was always a long shot in the Senate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 219-210 on a near party-line vote, but the Senate — where the majority held only 52 of 100 seats against a 60-vote threshold for most bills — never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Judy Chu introduced the bill on July 7, 2022, two weeks after the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision overturned Roe v. Wade, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
It never received a committee markup; leadership instead brought it straight to the floor under a rule reported July 13, packaged with several other bills, with one hour of debate.
On July 15, a Republican motion to recommit — sending the bill back to committee — failed 209-218, with all 209 voting Republicans in favor and all 218 voting Democrats against.
Final passage followed the same lines: 219-210, with 219 of 220 voting Democrats in favor, one Democrat opposed, and all 209 voting Republicans opposed.
The Senate received the bill on July 18, 2022, and no committee action, debate, or vote ever followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State abortion bans and restrictions in force at the time stayed on the books, and senators who opposed federal abortion protections never had to cast a vote on it. People in restriction states gained nothing during this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was almost perfectly partisan: 219 of 220 voting Democrats voted yes and all 209 voting Republicans voted no (219-210), and the motion to recommit failed on the identical 209-218 party split.

industries.note: The bill guarantees providers a statutory right to offer abortion care free of abortion-specific regulations — facility mandates, hospital privileges, telemedicine limits — and gives them standing to sue states, with attorney's fees. Their interest in staying open runs directly alongside patients' interest in access.

The bill bars states from limiting providers' ability to prescribe abortion drugs under evidence-based regimens or to provide services via telemedicine beyond rules that apply to telemedicine generally, opening the door to remote care in restriction states.

States lose the power to restrict abortion, face suits from the Justice Department and private plaintiffs with no immunity defense, and would have to dismantle restrictions already enacted. Officials deputized to enforce restrictions would be treated as government actors subject to those suits.
